newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FOCUS - Venezuela labor deal sketchy, but welcome.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Venezuela labor deal sketchy, but welcome.

text.p: An agreement to reform Venezuela's severance pay system, reached over the weekend, marks the beginning of a long-awaited freeing-up of Venezuela's rigid labor markets and represents a breakthrough after years of stalled negotiations, analysts said.

And although it comes with an inflationary price and crucial pieces are still lacking from the historic deal hammered out on Saturday between government, union and private sector leaders, analysts have so far welcomed the pact.
Details are still sketchy, but: "It's looking good," said Robert Bottome of VenEconomy financial magazine.
The first achievement of the deal, news of which surprised Venezuelans Monday morning, is that it was even reached.
"Labor and government have been talking, or not talking, about these reforms for years. In that sense, the mere fact they reached agreement is a victory," said labor specialist Victorino Marquez.
Second, the agreement eliminates a retroactivity clause which meant annual severance payments were calculated based on an employee's most recent wage, so impeding wage rises.
"With the end of the retroactivity clause, employers no longer have that excuse, which they've touted for years, for not increasing real wages," said Marquez.

Many see the reform as paving the way for a vital restructuring of Venezuela's bloated 1.2 million strong public sector. However, employers first have to meet old severance pay liabilities, which could exceed 3.5 trillion bolivars ($7 billion), according to past Finance Ministry estimates. Employees will be paid a month's salary, plus up to 200,000 bolivars in "bonuses," for each year worked, up to a limit of nine years for the private sector and 11 for the public.
Although the payments will be staggered -- workers receiving 25 percent over the next nine months, with the rest paid within five years -- analysts say they could have a huge inflationary impact.

"The government's revised target of 35 percent inflation (for 1997) looks increasingly unrealistic," said New York based IDEA in a market comment, adding that as fiscal policy remained lax, tight monetary policy -- most notably a strong bolivar -- would have to bear the inflation-fighting burden.

In an interview Monday with Union Radio, Planning Minister Teodoro Petkoff said the deal was nevertheless worth the higher inflation. "Even if it reaches 40 percent, inflation will still be much lower than (103 percent) last year," he said.
Not all employers were sure, however. And in a straw poll many also questioned the burden the new system placed on them.
Under the new plan workers will receive 45 days of severance pay after the first year's work, 60 days after two and another two days for each year worked up to a maximum of 90 days.

"That look's pretty expensive to me ... although the retroactivity is gone, and there's a 90 day ceiling, previously I only had to pay one month for each year worked," said a mining company executive.

Unlike the previous system, the payments will also be paid annually in a form chosen by the employee -- either as cash, or into a pension fund. The problem is that "the pension funds aren't yet even worked-out," said labor specialist Marquez.
"We still don't know how the new system will be implemented; the regulations are unclear, and that's so important especially in a country like Venezuela," said Marquez.
Nevertheless, the deal is a measure of how far Venezuela has come since government and labor leaders briefly reached a wage pact in 1995 which ended in disaster, analysts said.

Petkoff said the reforms would require complementary changes in Venezuela's Labor Law and Social Security System. But as the agreement had union backing, it could be passed by Congress as early as May 1.
President Rafael Caldera is to formally sign the agreement Monday evening, when further details will be released.
((-- Caracas newsroom, 582 505 2600))
